title: Distributed Periodic Scheduling with Cron
subtitle: Make each scheduled launch identifiable and recoverable
summary: Pip’s scheduler leader disappears after submitting a report. A replacement must distinguish missing work from an ambiguous duplicate. Replicated launch state, identifiable occurrences, and inspectable external outcomes matter because recording intent cannot make an external action atomic.

concepts.title: Launch semantics and idempotency
concepts.body: Pip safely repeats cleanup but must not send the harbor newsletter twice. Idempotency means repetition adds no unintended effect beyond the first successful execution. Jobs differ in tolerance for duplicates and omissions; the chapter generally prefers a missed launch over an ambiguous duplicate. Pip assigns outcome monitoring and recovery choices to job owners.

concepts.title: Synchronous replicated launch state
concepts.body: Pip’s elected leader records a launch beginning through consensus before contacting the external scheduler. It records completion of the attempt afterward, leaving followers enough state for failover. A replacement sees an unfinished 09:00 occurrence. Pip ensures the old leader stops external interaction when leadership ends so two leaders cannot launch it.

concepts.title: Reconciling partial external operations
concepts.body: Pip’s leader crashes after submitting report-0900 but before recording success. Replicated intent does not atomically cover an external side effect. The successor needs idempotency or reliable outcome inspection. Pip uses a precomputed occurrence-specific name to find running or completed work and submit only missing pieces.

concepts.title: State durability and dependency design
concepts.body: Pip restores scheduling from a snapshot plus later log entries. The replicated log preserves recent decisions; snapshots compact history for practical reconstruction. Small critical state stays with cron and snapshots receive separate protection, reducing normal dependence on general storage. Pip checks failure-domain placement and recovery speed because late failover can still miss frequent jobs.

misconceptions.claim: Consensus alone guarantees every external job executes exactly once.
misconceptions.correction: External submission can fail partway; recovery still needs idempotency or unambiguous outcome lookup.

misconceptions.claim: The job name alone uniquely identifies a cron launch.
misconceptions.correction: A recurring job has many occurrences, so its scheduled time or equivalent occurrence identifier must be included.

scenario.title: Reconcile a billing launch
scenario.context: A scheduler leader submits the 09:00 billing job, then fails before recording completion. The external scheduler can look up jobs by a unique occurrence identifier.

options.label: Look up the recorded occurrence before continuing
options.benefit: The successor can distinguish existing work from a missing submission.
options.cost: External outcome lookup must be reliable and include completed jobs.
options.consequence: The new leader finds billing-0900 and avoids submitting that occurrence again.

options.label: Submit again whenever completion is missing
options.benefit: This quickly covers submissions that genuinely never happened.
options.cost: A missing local completion record does not prove no external job ran.
options.consequence: The same billing occurrence may execute twice and produce duplicate effects.

scenario.debrief: A durable schedule is insufficient when submission can succeed just before the leader fails. Identify each occurrence and reconcile the external result; a concurrency lock alone does not prevent a completed billing run from being charged again later.

quiz.question: Why must launch intent reach a quorum before the external submission?
options: To ensure a successor knows the attempt may already have occurred
To ensure the external job finishes before the scheduled launch is acknowledged
To let any follower submit the job without first becoming leader
quiz.explanation: Otherwise failover can repeat an invisible launch.

quiz.question: A leader crashes after submission but before recording completion. What enables safe reconciliation?
options: Assuming every timeout means no submission happened
An idempotent submission or reliable lookup of that occurrence
quiz.explanation: The scheduler needs evidence about the external effect, not merely its own log.

quiz.question: Why include scheduled time in a launched job’s identity?
options: To require the external scheduler to execute all jobs in time order
To distinguish separate occurrences of the same recurring job
To prevent duplicate application effects without outcome lookup
quiz.explanation: Occurrence identity prevents confusion between an earlier completion and an unfinished current launch.

exercise.title: Recover an ambiguous launch
exercise.prompt: A scheduler leader fails after submitting a recurring job but before logging completion. Describe the evidence its successor needs before acting.
